Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 1 \) and \( P(2) = 2 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( n \geq 3 \), \( P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod{n} \). Determine the maximum possible degree of \( P(x) \).
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 1$ and $P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod{n^2}$ for all positive integers $n > 1$. Determine the smallest possible degree of $P(x)$.

Alice has a collection of colored balls. She arranges them in a line such that no two adjacent balls are of the same color. Alice notices that any sequence of three consecutive balls contains all three colors. She also realizes that the sequence repeats every 7 balls. What is the minimum number of different colors Alice could be using?

Alice and Bob play a game on a $1000 \times 1000$ grid. Each cell can be colored either black or white. Alice starts by choosing a cell and coloring it black. Then, Bob and Alice alternate turns, with Bob always going first. On each turn, the current player colors one uncolored cell black if it is adjacent to at least one other black cell; otherwise, they pass and the other player colors one cell black. The game ends when no more cells can be colored. Alice wants to maximize the number of black cells at the end of the game, while Bob wants to minimize this number. If both players play optimally, what is the final number of black cells on the grid?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 2023$. Suppose further that for any positive integer $n$, the polynomial $P(x)$ has a root modulo $n$. That is, there exists an integer $a$ such that $P(a) \equiv 0 \pmod{n}$. What is the minimum degree of $P(x)$?

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2023 \). Suppose that for every integer \( k \), if \( P(k) \) is divisible by 2023, then \( k \) must also be divisible by 2023. Determine the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of integer coordinates. Alice chooses a set of points such that for any pair of points in the set, their Euclidean distance is irrational. Bob, knowing Alice's set, must color all points of the grid using a finite number of colors. Alice wins if there is a monochromatic line (an infinite straight line) passing through at least three points of her set. Determine the smallest integer $n$ such that no matter how Alice plays, Bob can always guarantee a win with $n$ colors.

Alice has two tetrahedra, each with faces numbered 1 through 4. She rolls both simultaneously and computes the probability of having an odd sum as her score. Then Bob rolls six standard six-sided dice and computes the probability of his sum being divisible by 3 to be his score. Assuming that each face of the dice is equally likely to be rolled, what is the difference of the two scores, if each is rounded to the nearest integer? (After determining the two scores, subtract Bob’s from Alice’s and round the result to the nearest integer.)

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = P(1) = 2023 \). Suppose further that for any integer \( k \), \( P(k) \equiv 2023 \pmod{k} \). Find the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 2023$. Suppose further that for every prime $p$, the polynomial $P(x)$ modulo $p$ has exactly $p-1$ distinct roots in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$. Find the smallest possible degree of $P(x)$.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 3 \). Additionally, let \( P(n) \) be divisible by 5 for all integers \( n \) that are powers of 5. Find the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Alice und Bob spielen ein Spiel auf einem 3x3-Gitter von Karten. Zu Beginn sind alle Karten umgedreht. Sie wechseln sich ab, indem sie eine Karte umdrehen, und wenn sie die einzige umgedrehte Karte in ihrer Zeile und Spalte ist, können sie sie wieder umdrehen. Alice beginnt. Wie viele Umklappungen sind nötig, um sicherzustellen, dass einer der Spieler die letzte Karte umdrehen kann?

Alice and Bob play a game with a deck of 100 cards numbered from 1 to 100. The game proceeds as follows: Alice chooses a number $n$ (where $2 \leq n \leq 100$) and sets the deck in order from $1$ to $n$, then shuffles the rest of the deck. Afterward, they take turns picking a card from the top of the deck. The first player to pick a card numbered exactly $n$ wins the game. If Alice goes first and both players play optimally, determine the number of values of $n$ for which Alice can guarantee a win.
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for any positive integer $n$, $f(n^3) = f(n) \cdot f(n+1) \cdot f(n+2)$. Prove that no other function satisfies this property.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients, such that for every prime number \( p \), the number of distinct prime factors of \( P(p) \) is at most 2. Suppose further that for every integer \( n \geq 2 \), \( P(n) \) has at least one prime factor greater than \( n \). Determine the maximum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 2023 \). Suppose further that \( P(x) \) has the property that for any prime number \( p \), if \( P(n) \) is divisible by \( p \), then \( n \) is divisible by \( p \). Determine the smallest possible value of \( |P(2)| + |P(3)| \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and for all integers \( n \), \( P(n) \) is divisible by the smallest prime divisor of \( n \). Find all possible values of \( P(1) \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an 8x8 chessboard. They take turns placing a knight on an unoccupied square, with Alice going first. The game ends when a player cannot place a knight because all squares that can be reached by the knight's move are occupied. If Alice places her knight on a corner square on her first move, what is the minimum number of knights she must place to ensure that no matter how Bob plays, he will not be able to make his 64th move?

Alice and Bob are playing a game on a 3x3 grid. They take turns placing one of the two symbols "A" or "B" in an empty cell. The game ends when a 2x2 subgrid contains the same symbols in all four cells. If Alice places "A" and Bob places "B", and the game is played optimally, what is the minimum number of moves that guarantees Alice wins the game?

A convex hexagon has sides of lengths 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8. The area of the convex hexagon is equal to the sum of the areas of two triangles having sides of lengths 3 and 4, and 5 and 6, respectively. What is the area of the hexagon?

Find all positive integers \( n \) such that there exist \( n \) pairwise coprime positive integers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \) satisfying the following conditions:

1. For each \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \), \( a_i > 1 \).
2. For each \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, n \), \( a_i \mid a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \ldots + a_n^2 \).

In the plane, consider a set of $2023$ distinct points $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_{2023}$, no three of which are collinear. For each pair of points $P_i, P_j$ where $i < j$, a vector $\vec{v}_{ij}$ is defined as the displacement from $P_i$ to $P_j$. Let $S$ be the set of all possible sums of any combination of these vectors, including the zero vector. What is the minimum number of points that must be removed from $S$ to ensure that no two remaining vectors have their midpoint at any of the remaining points in $S$?

Alice and Bob play a game on a regular octahedron with eight vertices. They start with a token placed at a random vertex. On each turn, a player rolls a fair six-sided die. If the roll is even, the token moves to an adjacent vertex along an edge; if the roll is odd, the token stays at the same vertex. The first player to land the token back at its starting vertex wins the game. If Alice rolls first, what is the probability that she wins the game?
Alice和Bob在一块无限大的棋盘上玩一个游戏。棋盘的每个格子都可以放一个硬币，硬币的两面都是正面朝上。Alice和Bob轮流操作，每次可以将任何一个硬币翻转。Alice先开始操作。当Alice无法继续操作时，Bob获胜。在游戏开始前，棋盘上已经放置了$n$个正面朝上的硬币，这些硬币的初始位置是预先确定的。请问：当$n$从0增加到$m$时，有多少个$n$使得Bob有必胜策略？

Consider a set of \( n \) distinct points in the plane, \( P = \{P_1, P_2, ..., P_n\} \). A line segment connecting any two points in \( P \) is called a chord. Let \( C \) be the set of all possible chords formed from \( P \). For any point \( Q \) in the plane not in \( P \), define the visibility of \( Q \) with respect to \( C \) as the number of chords in \( C \) that cross the line segment \( QP_i \) for some \( i \). 

What is the minimum value of \( n \) such that there exists a point \( Q \) in the plane not in \( P \) whose visibility is greater than or equal to \( n/2 \)?

Alice and Bob play a game on a 5 × 5 grid. Alice starts by placing a single coin in one of the 25 squares, then Bob takes turns either moving the coin up, down, left, or right by exactly one square. Alice wins if she can return the coin to its starting position after an even number of moves; otherwise, Bob wins. What's the smallest number of moves Bob must make to guarantee a win regardless of where Alice initially places the coin?

In the coordinate plane, let \(P\) be the set of all points with integer coordinates. Define a "jump" from a point \(A\) to a point \(B\) if and only if the line segment \(AB\) is perpendicular to the line \(y = x\), and the distance from \(A\) to \(B\) is an integer. A "jump sequence" starting at a point \(A\) is a sequence of points \(A = P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_n\) such that for each \(i\), there exists a "jump" from \(P_{i-1}\) to \(P_i\). A point \(C\) is called "reachable" from \(A\) if there exists a jump sequence from \(A\) to \(C\).

For how many points in \(P\) is it true that every point reachable from the origin \((0,0)\) is also reachable from \(C\)?

Alice and Bob play a game on an \( n \times n \) chessboard. They take turns placing non-attacking rooks (no two rooks can be in the same row or column). Alice starts the game and the first player to place a rook such that all remaining empty cells are attacked by at least one rook loses. Determine the smallest integer \( k \) such that for every integer \( n \geq k \), Bob has a winning strategy.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of points where each point is at integer coordinates. They take turns moving a token initially placed at the origin (0,0). In each move, a player must move the token to a point \((x', y')\) such that \(x'\) and \(y'\) are both integers and the distance from the token's current position to \((x', y')\) is exactly \(\sqrt{5}\). The player who cannot make a move loses. If Alice starts the game, determine the smallest number of moves Bob needs to guarantee a win, assuming both players play optimally.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$, $P(1) = 2$, and $P(2) = 3$. Suppose there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P(n) = 0$. Determine the smallest possible value of $n$.

A configuration of **n** pairwise intersecting circles in the plane is called a **finite-diamond-tessellation** if the following conditions are met:

1. Each circle must be tangent to exactly four others at pairwise distinct points.
2. No three points of tangency are collinear.
3. The interior regions of the circles form a connected set.

For how many integers \( n \) is there a finite-diamond-tessellation of \( n \) circles?

Alice, Bob, and Carol start at different points on a circular track that is 100 meters in circumference. Alice starts at the starting line and walks at a speed of 5 meters per minute clockwise. Bob starts at a point 20 meters clockwise from Alice and walks at a speed of 7 meters per minute counterclockwise. Carol starts at a point 40 meters clockwise from Alice and walks at a speed of 3 meters per minute clockwise. After how many minutes will Alice, Bob, and Carol all meet at the same point on the track for the first time?

There are \( n \) cities arranged in a circle, each city being directly connected by a bidirectional road to exactly three other cities. Given that every pair of cities has at most one direct road between them, determine the smallest integer \( n \) for which it is possible to construct such a network of cities and roads.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( k \), if \( P(k) \) is a prime number, then \( P(k+1) \) is also a prime number. Determine the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Consider a sequence of distinct positive integers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) where each integer \(a_i\) is chosen from the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 2n\}\). The sequence is said to be "balanced" if for every pair of indices \(i < j\) such that \(i + j\) is even, the sum \(a_i + a_j\) is also even. Determine the maximum value of \(n\) for which it is possible to construct a balanced sequence. Additionally, find a specific balanced sequence that achieves this maximum \(n\).

A function $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
f(f(n) + n) = 3n \quad \text{and} \quad f(19) = f(91)
\end{align*} for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Compute $f(1)$.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \), \( P(1) = 2 \), and for all integers \( x \), \( P(x+1) - P(x) \) is divisible by 3. Define a sequence \( (a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty} \) by setting \( a_n = P(n)^2 - P(n-1)P(n+1) \). Find all positive integers \( k \) such that \( a_k \) is a perfect square.

Let $P(x, y)$ be a point on the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ with $a > b > 0$. Suppose there exist two distinct points $A$ and $B$ on the ellipse such that $PA = PB = 2PQ$, where $Q$ is the midpoint of chord $AB$. Determine the ratio $\frac{a}{b}$ for which there exist exactly three such points $P$ on the ellipse.

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 3 \) and \( P(3) = 10 \). Suppose further that for any integer \( n \), the value \( P(n) \) is not divisible by 5. Determine the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \), and provide an explicit construction of such a polynomial of this minimum degree. Additionally, prove that no such polynomial of lower degree exists.
What is the smallest integer greater than 100 such that the multiplicative order of 2 modulo that integer is also a multiple of 10?

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients and degree 2024. Suppose that \( P(1) = 2 \), \( P(2) = 5 \), and for all integers \( k \geq 3 \), \( P(k) = k^2 + 3 \). Determine the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( P(n) = n \).

Let \(P(x)\) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(0) = 1\). Suppose that for any integer \(n\), the equation \(P(n) = 0\) has at least one integer root. Prove that there exists a positive integer \(k\) such that \(P(k) = k!\).

The vertices of triangle \(ABC\) have integer coordinates. Consider all triangles whose vertices lie on the sides of \( \triangle ABC \) and whose sides are parallel to the \( x \)-axis and the \( y \)-axis. Among all such triangles, find the maximum possible area.
Find all triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers such that $a^3 + b^3 + c^3$ is a perfect square and $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = (a + b + c)^2.$

Find all integers \( n \geq 2 \) such that there exist integers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n \geq 1 \) for which the following conditions are satisfied:
- \( a_1 < a_2 < \ldots < a_n \)
- For all pairs \( (i, j) \) with \( 1 \leq i < j \leq n \), \( a_i a_j \) is a multiple of \( a_i + a_j \).

Prove your claim.

In a universe \( \mathcal{U} \) consisting of 1002 points, each pair of points is either connected by a red edge or a blue edge. Assume that for any set of 501 points, the number of red edges among them is at least the number of blue edges. Determine the minimum number of red edges that must exist in \( \mathcal{U} \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite number line. Alice starts at position 0. In each turn, Alice rolls a fair six-sided die. If she rolls an even number, she moves that many units to the right; if she rolls an odd number, she moves that many units to the left. Bob starts at position 10. He decides his own strategy. On his turn, Bob must choose to move exactly \(k\) units to the left or \(k\) units to the right, where \(k\) is any non-negative integer. The game ends when Alice and Bob meet at the same point on the number line. What is the smallest value of \(k\) such that Bob can guarantee they will meet at some point, no matter how Alice plays?
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$, $P(1) = 2$, and $P(n)$ is divisible by $n$ for every positive integer $n$. Find the minimum possible value of $|P(100)|$.

Alice and Bob play a game on a \( 100 \times 100 \) grid of unit squares. Alice starts by coloring one square red. Then, the players alternate turns, with Bob always moving first. On his turn, Bob chooses two adjacent squares in a row, column, or diagonal and colors them both red. On Alice’s turn, she colors three adjacent squares in a row, column, or diagonal red, with the condition that these three squares must already be partially surrounded by red squares (i.e., there must be at least one red square adjacent to each of the three squares being colored red). The game ends when no more moves are possible. Alice wins if every square on the grid is red at the end of the game. For which values of \( n \), does Alice have a winning strategy?

In a plane, there are 2023 points, no three of which are collinear. Each pair of points is connected by a line segment. A "painting" of these points consists of assigning one of three colors (red, blue, green) to each point such that no two points of the same color are connected by a line segment. Given that at least one such painting exists, determine the maximum number of points that can be colored red such that there still exists a valid painting. You may use the fact that for a set of points S in the plane with no three points collinear, there always exists a painting with the above properties.

Let $P(x)$ be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 2023$ and $P(n)$ is prime for all positive integers $n > 1$. Suppose further that $P(x)$ can be written as the product of two non-constant polynomials with integer coefficients, each of degree at least 1. Find the smallest possible degree of $P(x)$.

In a rectangular grid of 10 by 10 cells, some cells are colored black while the others remain white. Define a “region” as a maximal contiguous set of black cells (horizontally or vertically adjacent, but not diagonally). We call a region “reachable” from another if there exists a path of black cells (moving horizontally or vertically) that connects the two regions, without visiting any white cells.

Starting with an initial configuration where only one cell is colored black, we repeatedly perform an operation: choose any two adjacent (horizontally or vertically) white cells and color them black. The goal is to achieve a configuration where all black regions are reachable from each other. What is the minimum number of operations required to reach such a configuration?

Alice and Bob are playing a game on a \(10 \times 10\) grid. Alice starts by placing a single token on any square of the grid. The players take turns moving the token from its current position to an adjacent square, either horizontally or vertically. Each player must move the token to a new square with every turn. If a player cannot make a move that follows these rules, they lose. Alice moves first.

A move is considered valid if the token is moved to a square that has not been occupied by the token in the past two moves. If the token is moved to a square previously occupied in the last two moves, the player cannot make that move and loses the game.

For example, if Alice places the token on square (3,3), Bob moves it to (4,3), and Alice moves it to (4,2), then Bob must move it to a square other than (4,3) or (3,4) on his next turn.

Determine all initial positions on the grid from which Alice can force a win under optimal play by both players. What is the total number of such winning initial positions?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for any positive integer \( n \), the value of \( P(n) \) is a perfect square if and only if \( n \) is a perfect square. Determine the number of such polynomials \( P(x) \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, and let \( Q(x) = x^2 - 2x + 2 \). Suppose that for some integer \( n > 1 \), \( P(n) \) is a perfect square and \( P(n+1) \) is also a perfect square. Given that \( P(1) = 1 \), find all possible values of \( n \) for which \( P(x) \) divides \( Q(x) - x^2 \).

In the plane, consider a set of \( n \) distinct points. These points are to be connected by line segments such that no three segments intersect at a single point other than at the endpoints, and every point is connected to exactly three other points. For each point, a positive integer is assigned, and each segment’s color is determined by the sum of the integers of its endpoints modulo 4. Determine the largest possible value of \( n \) for which there exists such a configuration where all four colors (representing the residues 0, 1, 2, and 3 modulo 4) are used on at least one segment, and prove your claim.

Let $P(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c$ be a cubic polynomial with integer coefficients. Suppose that $P(1)$ is a prime number and that the roots of $P(x)$ are distinct integers. Determine the number of possible values for $c$.

Suppose \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}\) are positive integers satisfying \(\frac{1}{2a_{i}}+\frac{1}{2a_{j}} =\frac{1}{a_{k}}\) for some positive integer \(k\), where \(i \ne j\) and \(i,j,k\) are distinct. Let the maximum possible value of the least common multiple of the sum \(a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_{100}\) and the sum of all distinct elements among \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}\) be \(M\). What is the greatest integer that divides \(M\) for all valid sequences \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}\)?

Alice and Bob are playing a game with a pile of marbles. The pile starts with \( n \) marbles. Alice and Bob take turns removing marbles from the pile. On each turn, a player must remove either 1, 3, or 5 marbles. The player who takes the last marble wins. Given that both Alice and Bob play optimally, determine the smallest value of \( n \) such that Bob wins if Alice goes first.

Let $p(x)$ be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(0) = 1$ and $p(1) = 2023$. Suppose that for any prime number $q$, the equation $p(x) = q$ has at least one integer solution. Find the smallest possible degree of $p(x)$.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for all integers \( x \), \( P(x) \) is divisible by the largest power of 3 less than or equal to \( x \). Determine the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

A modified knight on an infinite chessboard moves according to the usual L shape of a knight, except it can perform up to n moves in total, where each move m (0 <= m < n) is chosen with probability proportional to (2m - 1) / n. For what smallest positive integer n can the modified knight start at any given square and reach any other square on the board with non-zero probability?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \), \( P(1) = 2 \), and for every integer \( n \geq 2 \), \( P(n) \) is divisible by \( n \). Find all possible values of \( P(2) \).

Find the number of ordered pairs \((a, b)\) of positive integers such that \(a\) is a multiple of 5, \(b\) is a multiple of 11, and the sum \(a + b\) is less than or equal to 2023, but \(a^2 + b^2\) is a perfect square. Then determine how many of these pairs \((a, b)\) satisfy the additional constraint that the integer \(\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) is a prime number.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 1 \) and \( P(n) \equiv n \pmod{p} \) for all integers \( n \), where \( p \) is a fixed prime number greater than 2. Determine the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \) when \( p \) is given.

Let \(P(x)\) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(0) = 1\) and \(P(1) = 2023\). Define the sequence \((a_n)\) by \(a_0 = 0\) and \(a_{n+1} = P(a_n)\) for all \(n \geq 0\). Suppose that for every positive integer \(k\), there exists a positive integer \(m\) such that \(a_m\) is divisible by \(k\). Determine the minimum possible degree of \(P(x)\).

Alice, Bob, and Carl play a game involving selecting non-empty subsets of the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}\). The game proceeds in turns where Alice picks a non-empty subset \(A_0\), then Bob picks a non-empty subset \(B_0\), followed by Carl picking a non-empty subset \(C_0\). The game continues indefinitely with players alternating colors (Alice and Carl play white, Bob plays black) and selecting subsets based on the previous player's choice.

At the end of the game, two sums are computed:
- The white sum is the count of positive integers \(x\) that belong to \(A_0\), \(A_2\), \(A_4\), etc., but not to \(A_1\), \(A_3\), \(A_5\), etc.
- The black sum is the count of positive integers \(x\) that belong to \(B_1\), \(B_3\), \(B_5\), etc., but not to \(B_0\), \(B_2\), \(B_4\), etc.

The first player to make their sum equal to the other player's sum loses. Determine all possible sets \(A_0\) such that Alice can always win regardless of the strategies employed by Bob and Carl.

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 2023 \) and \( P(2) = 2024 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( n \), \( P(n) \) is divisible by at least one of the numbers \( 1, 2, \ldots, n \). Determine the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of unit squares. Initially, Alice places a single token at the origin (0, 0). Then, they take turns performing moves, starting with Alice. In each turn, a player can move the token to any of the eight adjacent squares (up, down, left, right, or diagonally) that are still unoccupied. If a player cannot make a move, they lose. Assuming both players play optimally, who has a winning strategy, and what is the minimum number of moves required for the first player to guarantee a win?

Alice and Bob are playing a game on a 10x10 grid. They take turns placing stones of their own color on the grid, with Alice starting. Each player can place one stone per turn. If a player can place a stone such that it forms a 2x2 square (or any other square) with any other stones already placed on the board, they lose. The game ends when one player loses or all squares are filled. Assuming optimal play, who has a winning strategy?

Four concentric circles have radii in arithmetic progression with common difference $r$. The areas of the annuli formed by the first and second circles and by the third and fourth circles are in the ratio $3:5$. Find the smallest possible integer value of the sum of the radii of the four circles.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 1$ and $P(2) = 3$. Suppose further that for every integer $n$, the number $P(n)P(n+1)$ is divisible by some fixed prime $p$. Determine all possible values of $p$ for which this condition holds.

A lattice point in the plane is called **visible** if there does not exist another lattice point on the line segment connecting the origin and it. Let \( S \) be the set of all visible lattice points in the first quadrant. We say that a non-empty subset \( A \) of \( S \) is **complete** if for any distinct points \( P \) and \( Q \) in \( A \), the point \((P + Q)/2\) is also in \( A \). Find the maximum possible size of a complete subset of \( S \).

Alice and Bob are playing a game on an \(n \times n\) grid of cells, each cell initially containing a single pebble. They take turns removing pebbles from the grid, with Alice going first. On each turn, a player must remove at least one pebble and at most \(k\) pebbles from any row or column they choose. The player who is unable to make a move loses the game. Determine the smallest integer \(k\) such that for any \(n \geq 3\), Alice can guarantee a win regardless of how Bob plays.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that \( P(x) \) has no integer roots. Define the sequence \( \{a_n\} \) by \( a_1 = 1 \) and \( a_{n+1} = P(a_n) \) for all \( n \geq 1 \). If there exists an integer \( k \geq 1 \) such that \( a_k \) is divisible by 2023, find the minimum possible value of \( k \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(n) \) divides \( n! \) for all positive integers \( n \). Suppose further that \( P(x) \) has no real roots. Prove that \( P(x) \) cannot have more than two distinct integer roots.

Given a polynomial \( Q(x) \) with integer coefficients such that \( Q(0) = 1 \) and \( Q(n) \) divides \( n! \) for all positive integers \( n \), and that \( Q(x) \) has no real roots. Prove that \( Q(x) \) cannot have more than two distinct integer roots.

For any positive integer \( k \) and any nonzero integer \( a \), let \( S(k, a) \) denote the set of integers \( n \) such that \( P(n) = ka \). Given that for all \( k \geq 1 \) and nonzero integers \( a \), \( S(k, a) \) has exactly one element, find the value of \( P(-1) \).

Now, consider the polynomial \( R(x) \) defined by \( R(x) = P(x) \cdot Q(x) \). If \( R(x) \) has no real roots and \( R(0) = 1 \), and given that \( R(n) \) divides \( n! \) for all positive integers \( n \), prove that \( R(x) \) cannot have more than four distinct integer roots.

What is the smallest positive integer value of $n$ for which there exists a set of integers $\{x_1, x_2, ..., x_n\}$, such that $x_i \equiv i \pmod{2024}$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, and at the same time, every possible difference $|x_i - x_j|$ for distinct $i, j$ in $\{1, 2, ..., n\}$ is unique and no smaller than 2024?

In the Cartesian plane, consider a set \(S\) of points \((x, y)\) such that \(x\) and \(y\) are both integers and \(0 \leq x, y \leq 2024\). Define a move from a point \((x, y)\) to \((x + 1, y + 2)\) or \((x, y + 1)\), but only if the destination point is within \(S\). Starting from \((0, 0)\), what is the maximum number of moves that can be made without revisiting any point?

In the Cartesian plane, consider a regular octagon \( P_1P_2P_3P_4P_5P_6P_7P_8 \) with side length 2 inscribed in the unit circle centered at the origin. A point \( Q \) is chosen uniformly at random inside the unit circle. Let \( d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_8 \) be the distances from \( Q \) to the sides of the octagon. Determine the probability that \( d_1 + d_2 + \ldots + d_8 \leq 4 \).

In a circular arrangement of $n$ cells, two players, $A$ and $B$, alternately place a unique, non-zero integer into each empty cell. The game ends when all cells are filled. The score of each player is calculated as the absolute difference between the sums of their respective groups of consecutive, non-overlapping integers. Player $A$ wins if their score is strictly greater than that of $B$. For which smallest value of $n > 2$ is it guaranteed that player $B$ can always prevent $A$ from winning, regardless of the order in which the cells are filled?

Write $n$.

Given a sequence of positive integers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100} \) such that \( a_{i+1} = a_i^2 + 1 \) for all \( i = 1, 2, \ldots, 99 \), and knowing that \( a_1 \) is a prime number greater than 100, find the smallest possible value of \( a_1 \) such that the sum \( S = a_1 + a_2 + \ldots + a_{100} \) is divisible by 3.

Alice and Bob play a game with two distinct integers chosen randomly from 1 to 1000. Alice selects one integer and Bob selects another. Their goal is to minimize the absolute difference between the squares of their chosen numbers without communicating with each other. Assuming optimal strategies by both players, what is the largest possible minimum difference in the squares of their chosen numbers?

Alice and Bob play a game on a circular board that is divided into 12 equally sized sectors labeled from 1 to 12. They take turns placing a marker into any empty sector, starting with Alice. If a player places a marker such that there are three consecutive numbers (in a circular manner) with markers in the three sectors, they lose the game. For example, if Alice places a marker in sector 1, and then Bob places a marker in sector 4, Alice will lose if she next places a marker in sector 7.

What is the minimum number of markers that must be placed before the game is certain to be over?

Alice and Bob play a game on a complete graph with 10 vertices. Alice labels each edge with a distinct integer from 1 to 45. Bob can select any subset of the vertices, and for each selected vertex, he finds the sum of the labels of all edges incident to that vertex. What is the minimum number of vertices Bob must select to ensure that, no matter how Alice labels the edges, he can determine with certainty the sum of the labels of all 45 edges?

Let \( S = \{1, 2, \ldots, 2024\} \) be a set of integers. For any non-empty subset \( A \subseteq S \), define \( f(A) \) as the number of elements in \( A \) that are divisible by at least one element of \( S \). Determine the minimum possible value of \( f(A) \) over all subsets \( A \) of \( S \) of size 1012.
Let \(P(x)\) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(0) = 1\) and for all integers \(n\), \(P(n)\) divides \(P(P(n)) + n\). Find all possible values of \(P(2023)\).

Alice plays a game on the plane where she takes a $2021 \times 2021$ grid. She assigns to each grid cell a real number from 0 to 1. Her goal is to minimize the sum of squares of the numbers in any 2x2 square of the grid. What is the minimum possible value she can achieve?

Let P(x) be a polynomial with integer coefficients. Suppose that for some fixed integer k, P(k) = 2023, and for every integer n, P(n) is divisible by k-1 or k+1. Find the maximum possible degree of P(x).

Hint: Consider the properties of polynomials with integer coefficients and their behavior at integer points.

An infinite sequence \((a_n)\) is defined by \(a_1 = 1\) and for all \(n \geq 1\), \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest positive integer such that the sum of the first \(n+1\) terms of the sequence is a perfect square, and \(a_{n+1} > a_n\). Let \(S\) be the set of all positive integers \(k\) such that \(a_k\) divides \(k!\). Determine the largest element of \(S\).
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all real numbers $x$ and $y$, the inequality $$f(x^2 + y^2) \leq f(x + y) + |xy|$$ holds.

Alice and Bob play a game on a $2023 \times 2023$ grid, with Alice going first. On their turn, a player can choose a cell that has not been colored yet and color it black, with the following rules:

- If it is Alice's turn, she can color any cell she wishes.
- If it is Bob's turn, he can only color a cell that is either in the same row or the same column as the previously colored cell, and is not adjacent to any cell he has already colored.

What is the maximum number of cells Alice can guarantee to color if both players play optimally?
Find all polynomials \( P(x) \) with real coefficients such that for every integer \( n \), the value \( P(n) \) is a perfect square if and only if \( n \) is a perfect square.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( n \), the value \( P(n) \) is a perfect square. Determine the maximum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = P(1) = 2023 \). Suppose further that for any integer \( n \), if \( P(n) \) is divisible by 2023, then \( P(n+1) \) is not divisible by 2023. Given these conditions, find the largest positive integer \( k \) such that for every integer \( n \geq k \), the value \( P(n) \) modulo 2023 is unique. That is, \( P(n) \not\equiv P(m) \pmod{2023} \) whenever \( n \neq m \) and both are at least \( k \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an $n \times n$ grid. Alice starts by choosing a square in the bottom left corner of the grid. Then, they take turns placing a token on any unoccupied square such that the distance from the token to any existing token is exactly $\sqrt{2}$. If no such square exists when it is Alice's turn, she loses. If she wins, she gets to choose another starting square and place her token, then Bob goes again, and they continue in this manner until Alice loses. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum possible number of turns Alice can make before losing, if both players play optimally. Find the smallest value of $n$ such that $f(n) > 2023$.
What is the smallest positive integer k such that for any coloring of the integers from 1 to 100 with 3 colors, there exists an arithmetic progression of length k with all terms of the same color?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 1$ and $P(n)$ is prime for all positive integers $n$. Define $Q(x) = P(P(x))$. If $Q(2)$ is also prime, find the maximum number of distinct prime values that can be obtained by evaluating $Q(n)$ for all integers $1 \leq n \leq 100$.

Find all functions \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \) such that for all real numbers \( x \) and \( y \),
\[
f(x^2 + yf(x) + 1) = xf(x) + f(y) + 2.
\]

Let $P(x)$ be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. Suppose that for all prime numbers $p$ and positive integers $k$, the value $P(p^k)$ is divisible by $p$. If $P(x)$ has no integer roots, prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for any integer $a$, the value $P(a)$ is divisible by some prime number less than $N$.

Consider a 2023 × 2023 grid where each cell is initially empty. In a move, you select a row or column, then flip the state of each cell (empty → filled, filled → empty) in the chosen row or column. The game ends when the grid has exactly one empty cell. Determine the minimum number of moves required to achieve this state, regardless of the initial configuration of the grid. Prove your answer.

Let $P$ be a convex polygon with integer coordinates inscribed in a circle centered at $(0,0)$ with radius $r$. Let $n$ denote the number of sides of $P$. We define $S$ as the sum of the absolute values of the products of the $x$-coordinates and $y$-coordinates of all possible subsets of $n-1$ vertices of $P$ (including the empty subset). Determine the minimum value of $S$ over all possible polygons $P$ for a given $n$.

Alice, Bob, and Carol play a game on a closed curve $\gamma$ in the plane. The curve is defined parametrically by the functions $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. Each player chooses a continuous point $P_i$ on $\gamma$ for $i = A, B, C$. The scoring system is as follows:

- Each point $P_i$ is worth the length of the arc of $\gamma$ between the closest points $P_j$ (for $j \neq i$).
- The total score of a player is the sum of the lengths of the arcs assigned to their chosen point.
  
Alice, Bob, and Carol aim to maximize their scores. They decide to place their points at distinct values of $t$. Given that the parametric curve $\gamma(t) = (t^3 - 3t, t^2)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$ and assuming they play optimally, determine the maximum combined score of the three players.

Let $P$ be a permutation of the set $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2n\}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. Define the *swap-value* of $P$, denoted by $S(P)$, as the minimum number of adjacent transpositions required to sort $P$. Now, let $D(P)$ be the number of pairs $(i, j)$ with $1 \leq i < j \leq 2n$ such that $P_i > P_j$. Prove or disprove: For every permutation $P$, the swap-value $S(P)$ is bounded below by $\frac{D(P)}{n}$. Moreover, find the minimum value of $n$ for which there exists a permutation $P$ such that $S(P) = \frac{D(P)}{n}$.

Let \(P(x)\) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(0) = 1\) and \(P(1) = 3\). Suppose that for every prime number \(p\), there exists an integer \(k_p\) such that \(P(k_p) \equiv 0 \pmod{p}\) but \(P(k_p + 1) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}\). If \(P(n)\) has exactly 12 distinct prime factors for some integer \(n\), find the minimum possible degree of \(P(x)\).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 2 \), \( P(2) = 3 \), and \( P(3) = 5 \). Define the sequence \( \{a_n\} \) by \( a_n = P(n) \) for \( n \geq 1 \). Suppose \( a_n \) is a prime number for all \( n \geq 1 \). Determine the smallest possible value of \( a_6 \).

Given a set of n points P1, P2, ..., Pn on the plane such that for any two points, there exists a circle passing through both with center C. Find all possible values of n for which there exists a circle C such that the set of all points {C, C', C'', ..., C^(n-1)} forms a convex polygon with sides C'C', C''C'', ..., C^(n-1)C', C'C'' where C' and C'' are the midpoints of segments P1P2 and P2P3 respectively and C^k denotes the k-th iterate of the function f(x) = 2x modulo 1 for real x.

Alice and Bob play a game on a chessboard with N squares on each side. They take turns placing non-overlapping squares of side length k on the board, where k is a positive integer such that 1 ≤ k ≤ N. The first player who cannot place a square on the board loses. Alice goes first.

Determine, for each N, the smallest value of k such that the first player (Alice) has a guaranteed winning strategy.
Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(0) = p(1) = 2023$ and $p(n) \equiv n \pmod{2023}$ for all integers $n$. Find the minimum possible positive value of $p(2024)$.

Alice and Bob play a game on a grid of \(1000 \times 1000\). Alice starts at the bottom-left corner, and Bob starts at the top-right corner. Each turn, Alice can move either one unit up or one unit right, and Bob can move either one unit down or one unit left. Alice and Bob take turns, with Alice going first. The game ends when one player reaches the point directly diagonally opposite to their starting point. What is the probability that Alice reaches the ending point before Bob?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$, $P(1) = 2$, and $P(2) = 3$. Suppose further that for every integer $n$, $P(n)$ is divisible by some prime $p_n$ that does not divide $P(k)$ for $k < n$. What is the minimum possible degree of $P(x)$?

Alice plays a game with an \(n \times n\) grid of lightbulbs. Each lightbulb can be in one of two states: off or on. Alice can perform three types of operations:

1. Select a row and toggle the state of all \(n\) bulbs in that row.
2. Select a column and toggle the state of all \(n\) bulbs in that column.
3. Select a diagonal (either main or anti-main) and toggle the state of all \(n\) bulbs in that diagonal.

If the grid starts with all bulbs off, what is the minimum number of operations Alice needs to make all bulbs on if \(n\) is a prime number? Additionally, determine whether it's possible for Alice to return the grid to the all-off state by performing any sequence of operations after having at least one bulb on.

Alice and Bob are playing a game with a sequence of complex numbers defined recursively as follows: \(z_1 = 1 + i\), and for \(n \geq 1\), \(z_{n+1} = \frac{2z_n}{1 - z_n^2}\). If after 2024 iterations, \(|z_{2024}|\) is of the form \(\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}}\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime positive integers, what is \(a + b\)?

Find all triples of positive integers (a,b,c) such that:

\[abc \mid a^4 + b^4 + c^2\]

and additionally, \[a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \mid a^4 + b^4 + c^4.\]

Find all functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+\) such that for all positive real numbers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) satisfying \(ab + bc + ca \leq 1\), the inequality \(f(a^2 + b^2 + c^2) \leq f(a) + f(b) + f(c)\) holds. Additionally, \(f\) is strictly increasing.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 2023$. Suppose further that for every integer $n$, $P(n)$ is divisible by $n^3 - n$ if and only if $n$ is a prime number. Find the minimum possible value of the degree of $P(x)$.

What is the maximum positive integer $k$ such that there exists a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfying the property that for any function $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with range $g(\mathbb{N}) = \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$ there exists a sequence of functions $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_k : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, \; f_n(n) = g(n).$$

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 2023 \) and \( P(2) = 2024 \). Suppose there exists a polynomial \( Q(x) \) with integer coefficients satisfying \( P(x) = (x-1)^3 Q(x) + x^2 + x + 1 \). Determine the minimum number of integer roots (counting multiplicities) that \( P(x) \) can have, and find the minimum possible value of \( P(0) + P(3) \).

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 2023$ and $P(2) = 3034$. Find the smallest positive integer $n$ for which there exists a set of $n$ distinct integers $a_1, a_2, ..., a_n$ such that $P(a_i) = 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ and the product $a_1 \cdot a_2 \cdot ... \cdot a_n$ is a perfect square.

A positive integer sequence is called _self-involving_ if for every positive integer  n, the number of terms that are exactly divisible by  n  is also equal to  n. Determine all possible values of  p - q, where  p  and  q  are two consecutive terms of the longest possible self-involving sequence.

Let \( f(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( f(0) = 1 \) and \( f(1) = 2023 \). If \( f(x) \) has no rational roots and the sum of the absolute values of its coefficients is a prime number, find the minimum number of terms in \( f(x) \).

Alice, Bob, and Carol are playing a game on a circle of 100 seats numbered 0 to 99. They start at seat 0. Each turn, the player tosses a fair coin. If it lands heads, they move clockwise by the number of seats rolled on a standard six-sided die; if tails, they move counterclockwise. The game ends when all three players occupy the same seat again for the first time. What is the probability that the game ends exactly after Alice’s first turn?

Alice and Bob play a game on a \(100 \times 100\) grid of unit squares, where initially all squares are white. Alice chooses a square and paints it blue. Then Bob chooses a square and paints it red. This process continues, with Alice choosing one of the remaining unpainted squares, followed by Bob choosing one of the remaining unpainted squares. The game ends when all squares are painted. Let \( A \) be the set of squares painted by Alice, and \( B \) be the set of squares painted by Bob. Alice wins if there is a continuous path of blue squares from the top row to the bottom row, such that any red square along this path forms a right-angled triangle with two blue squares, with the red square at the right angle. Find the smallest number of blue squares Alice can guarantee to paint so that she can win the game no matter how Bob responds.

Alice has a collection of 2024 cards, each containing a unique integer from 1 to 2024. She decides to play a game with her friend Bob, using the following rule: Alice chooses one card at random, and then Bob can either choose to double the number on Alice's card or to subtract 1 from it. If the number on the card after Bob's turn is a prime number, Bob wins; otherwise, Alice wins. Assume both players play optimally. What is the probability that Bob wins the game?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 2023$. Suppose further that for every integer $k$, there exists an integer $n$ such that $P(n)$ is divisible by $k$. Determine the minimum possible degree of $P(x)$.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of squares, each square initially colored either red or blue. The game starts with all squares red except for one square in the center, which is blue. In each turn, a player can change the color of any uncolored square to the opposite color of the majority color among its four immediate neighbors (up, down, left, right). If a square has no colored neighbors, it remains uncolored. The game ends when no more moves are possible. Determine the minimum number of turns required for the game to end, and describe a strategy for Alice to achieve this.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \), \( P(1) = 3 \), and \( P(2) = 7 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( k \), \( P(k) \) is a prime number when \( k \) is a prime, and a composite number otherwise. Determine the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

A configuration consists of three distinct segments on a plane, with each segment potentially shared by vertices of multiple configurations. What is the maximum integer value of $n$ such that any given set of $n$ points in general position admits a configuration of exactly three segments that touch all $n$ points?

AIME competitor Jennifer is applying her combinatorics training to a new tile arrangement. She wishes to cover her dorm room floor with specially patterned square tiles such that each tile can be divided into four distinct quadrants, each of which has one of four unique designs. Each tile must exhibit exactly one of the 64 ways to arrange these designs in the four quadrants. The dorm room floor can be precisely divided into a 6x6 grid. Jennifer wants to tile the floor in such a way that the collection of arrangements for all tiles on the floor forms a configuration which exhibits rotational symmetry of 180 degrees about the floor's center. How many such valid arrangements are there?

Alice and Bob play a game on an \( n \times n \) grid. Initially, all cells are empty. Players take turns placing a coin in an empty cell, with Alice going first. The game ends when no more coins can be placed. If a coin is placed such that the number of coins in its row plus the number of coins in its column equals \( n \), Alice wins. Otherwise, Bob wins. Find the smallest value of \( n \) for which Alice has a winning strategy.

Alice is given a positive integer $n$ and told that $n$ is the difference of two consecutive perfect squares. What is the smallest possible value of $n$ for which the sum of the digits of $n$ is also a perfect square?

In the realm of modular arithmetic and number theory, consider the sequence \(\{a_n\}\) defined by \(a_1 = 2\) and \(a_{n+1} = a_n^2 - a_n + 1\). Determine the smallest positive integer \(k\) such that \(a_k \equiv 0 \pmod{p}\) for every prime \(p > 2\) where \(a_k\) is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers. Note that \(\{a_n\}\) forms a recursive sequence with rapid growth.

Alice, Bob, and Carol play a game with a bag containing n marbles, n > 1. They take turns to draw marbles from the bag one by one, until there are no marbles left. Each player always takes at most half of the remaining marbles in their turn. Furthermore, the sum of marbles taken by Alice and Bob must be even. When the game ends, how many of the possible value(s) for the total number of marbles in the bag satisfy the condition that Alice wins, regardless of how Bob and Carol play?

Let $p(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $p(0)=1$ and $p(1)=2023$. Suppose that there exist distinct integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2023}$ with $a_1 = 0$ and $a_2 = 1$ such that $p(x)$ has a rational root at $x = a_i$ for every $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 2023$. Determine the maximum possible number of rational roots that $p(x)$ can have, and prove that this number is indeed attainable by constructing an explicit polynomial that meets the given conditions.

Alice and Bob play a game on a board divided into a grid of \(20 \times 20\) cells. Alice starts by marking any number of cells with 'X'. Bob then marks cells with 'O' in such a way that every row and every column contains exactly 10 cells marked 'X' and 10 cells marked 'O'. Determine the minimum number of 'X' cells Alice must initially place to guarantee that Bob can always win regardless of how Alice places them.

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and for all integers \( n \geq 1 \), the following conditions are satisfied:
1. \( P(n) \) is divisible by \( n \).
2. If \( p \) is a prime number, then \( P(p) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2} \).

Determine all possible polynomials \( P(x) \) that meet these criteria.

Alice, Bob, and Carol are playing a game with a deck of cards numbered from 1 to 30. Each player draws a card without replacement until all cards have been drawn. Alice computes the sum of the numbers on the cards she drew. Bob computes the sum of the squares of the numbers on the cards he drew. Carol computes the sum of the products of pairs of numbers from the cards she drew. What is the minimum possible value of the maximum of the three computed numbers, over all possible ways of drawing the cards?

A rectangular prism has integer dimensions $l,$ $w,$ and $h.$ Its volume equals its surface area. There is a second rectangular prism with the same volume as the first, but different dimensions, where two of the dimensions are also integers, and the third dimension is an integer divided by a prime. How many such integer pairs $(l, w)$ exist?

Alice and Bob play a game on an \( n \times n \) grid where each square can contain either a 0 or 1. They start with all squares set to 0. Alice goes first and can choose any square and change it from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. Bob goes second and can only choose an unchosen square. Bob's goal is to ensure that no two squares in the same row or column are both 1 at any time. If Bob can achieve this, he wins; otherwise, Alice wins. What is the smallest value of \( n \) for which Bob has a winning strategy?

Alice is a value-minded merchant. She owns n objects of identical appearance but different values: v1, v2, ..., vn. She wants to arrange them in a line such that the number of different objects before each position is maximal among all arrangements of objects with no more than k=3 different objects in total. How should she arrange these n objects, knowing she will only trade up to two times with her brothers when they ask for a better offer? What is the optimal lower bound of average number of distinct objects she should see?

Alice and Bob play a game on a 10x10 grid. Each player takes turns placing stones on the grid, starting with Alice. Alice places stones of color red, and Bob places stones of color blue. The first player to create a vertical or horizontal line of 5 stones of their own color wins the game. After the game, the grid is examined, and it is found that Alice placed exactly 12 red stones and Bob placed exactly 13 blue stones. Determine the minimum number of horizontal or vertical lines of length 5 that must exist in the grid at this point.

In a regular polygon, the ratio of the longest diagonal to the shortest diagonal is exactly equal to the ratio of the side length to the radius of the circumscribed circle. Find all possible numbers of sides for such a polygon, given that the number of sides is more than 2 but less than 50.

Alice and Bob are playing a game on an infinitely long chessboard, starting at the origin (0, 0). The game involves a special piece called a "mathmage". The mathmage has the ability to move either:
1. Any even number of squares horizontally (left or right) or vertically (up or down)
2. Any odd number of squares diagonally

Alice starts with the mathmage and they take turns moving the piece. The player who cannot make a valid move loses. Given that Alice and Bob play optimally, what is the smallest possible value of n such that a new player, Charlie, would win if he were given the mathmage at move n (which could be 1, 2, 3, ...), assuming Charlie plays optimally?

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of unit squares. Alice places a red token at the origin \((0, 0)\). Then, they take turns moving the token. On a turn, the current player moves the token to a square that is one unit to the right, left, above or below its current position. Alice moves first. The game ends when the token lands on a square whose coordinates \((x, y)\) satisfy the condition that \(x^2 + y^2\) is a perfect square. Alice wins if the token lands on such a square; Bob wins otherwise.

Alice and Bob use the following strategy:
- Alice starts at \((0, 0)\) and moves to \((1, 0)\).
- On each of her moves, Alice always moves the token to the nearest square to the right or left that is exactly one unit away from any point \((x, y)\) for which \(x^2 + y^2\) is a perfect square.
- Bob's strategy is to always move the token in the opposite direction to Alice's intended move.

For how many positive integers \(n \leq 10^9\) does Alice have a guaranteed winning strategy regardless of Bob's moves, if she starts at \((0, n)\) instead of \((0, 0)\)?

Alice is playing a game with a deck of 52 cards, which includes one Joker. Each card has a unique value from 1 to 52, and there is a single Joker card. Alice randomly selects a card from the deck. If she picks the Joker, she wins a prize of $n$ dollars. If she picks any other card, she loses 1 dollar. Alice decides to play until she either wins or loses a total of 10 dollars. Determine the smallest integer value of $n$ such that Alice's expected value of winnings after 10 rounds is positive.

Define a sequence \( \{a_n\} \) by \( a_1 = 1 \) and for \( n \geq 2 \),
\[ a_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \left( a_k + a_{n-k} \right). \]

Let \( S \) be the set of all positive integers \( n \) for which \( a_n \) can be expressed as \( \frac{p}{q} \) with \( p \) and \( q \) being relatively prime positive integers and \( q \) is not divisible by any prime number \( < 100 \).

Find the number of elements in the set \( S \) that are less than or equal to 2023.

Consider a set S = {1, 2, ..., n} for some positive integer n. Define a "marked subset" of S as any subset of S that includes at least one element that is also a divisor of the sum of its elements. How many "marked subsets" are there if n = 12?

A regular dodecagon \( P_1P_2P_3\dotsb P_{12} \) is inscribed in a circle. The major arc \( P_1P_7 \) is divided into three equal parts by points \( X, Y, Z \). Determine the sum of ratios of the lengths of these arcs \( \frac{P_1X}{XZ} + \frac{P_1Y}{YZ} + \frac{P_1Z}{ZY} \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose that for every integer \( n \), \( P(n) \) is a perfect square. Determine the largest possible value of \( |P(-1)| \).
Find all positive integers \( n \) such that the polynomial \( P(x) = x^n + 2x^{n-1} + 3x^{n-2} + \cdots + (n+1) \) has exactly \( n \) distinct integer roots.

Let \( S \) be a subset of the set \( \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2023\} \) such that for any two distinct elements \( a, b \in S \), the greatest common divisor (gcd) of \( a \) and \( b \) is not equal to 1. What is the maximum number of elements that \( S \) can contain? Express your answer in terms of the smallest integer \( n \) such that the set \( \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, n\} \) has at least as many elements as \( S \).

(Note: The problem asks for the smallest \( n \) in terms of a function, which could be straightforward or more complex.)

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 2023$. Let $r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n$ be the distinct integer roots of $P(x)$, and let $S = \{r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n\}$. Define $Q(x)$ as the polynomial obtained by replacing each $r_i$ in $P(x)$ with $r_i + 1$. If $Q(0) = k$ for some positive integer $k$, find the maximum possible value of $|S|$ such that $k$ is also a prime number.

A sequence of positive integers \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots\) is defined such that for all \(n \geq 2\), \(a_n\) is the smallest integer greater than \(a_{n-1}\) that ensures the sum of any subset of the sequence (including the empty set, whose sum is defined as 0) is not a perfect square. Determine the smallest possible value of \(a_4\) if \(a_1 = 1\).

Alice, Bob, and Carol are each given a number, and they perform the following operation on their number repeatedly. Let’s denote their current numbers as $A_n$, $B_n$, and $C_n$ respectively at the $n$-th step, with initial values $A_0$, $B_0$, and $C_0$. They perform the following steps in order:

1. Alice computes her new number $A_{n+1}$ by replacing $A_n$ with $2A_n + B_n + C_n$.
2. Bob computes his new number $B_{n+1}$ by replacing $B_n$ with $B_n + 2C_n$.
3. Carol computes her new number $C_{n+1}$ by replacing $C_n$ with $C_n + A_n + B_n$.

If $A_0 = 2$, $B_0 = -1$, and $C_0 = 3$, determine after how many operations it will be the case that $A_n = B_n$.

There exists a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree at least 4, such that for every positive integer n, the sum of the first n terms of its corresponding sequence of integer coefficients is divisible by n. Prove that there exists infinitely many positive integers n for which this sum is divisible by n^2. Find the smallest possible degree of the polynomial.

Alice and Bob play a game on a 10x10 grid. Alice starts by choosing a square and coloring it black. Then, Bob chooses a row or a column and colors all squares in that row or column white. Alice then colors another square black, and the game continues in this manner. The game ends when Alice cannot make a move. Alice wins if there are exactly 20 black squares on the grid at the end; otherwise, Bob wins. What is the smallest number of squares that Alice must color black on her first move to guarantee a win?

Hint: Consider the effect of Bob's moves and how they affect the remaining available squares for Alice's future moves.

Alice and Bob play a game with a sequence of integers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2024}\) arranged in a line, where each integer is between 1 and 100, inclusive. Alice and Bob take turns selecting a number \(a_k\) (where \(k\) is the number of the turn) and reducing it by 1. If at any point, Alice selects a number and it becomes zero, Alice wins. If Bob manages to avoid selecting any zero numbers until Alice's turn after \(2024\) turns, Bob wins. Determine all pairs \((x, y)\) where Alice's strategy involves aiming for Alice to win when \(a_1 = x\) and Bob's strategy to always win when \(a_1 = y\). What is the sum of all distinct \(x\) values in such pairs?

Consider a sequence of positive integers \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots\) defined as follows: \(a_1 = 2\), and for each \(n \geq 1\), \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest integer greater than \(a_n\) such that for all \(1 \leq k \leq n\), the greatest common divisor (gcd) of \(a_{n+1}\) and \(a_k\) is exactly \(k\). Determine the value of \(a_{100}\).

Let $S$ be the set of positive integers that can be expressed as the sum of distinct Fibonacci numbers (where the Fibonacci sequence is defined by $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, and $F_{n} = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 3$). Define a function $f: S \to S$ such that $f(x)$ is the smallest integer in $S$ that can be formed by replacing one of the addends in $x$ with its successor in the Fibonacci sequence (if such a replacement is possible). For example, $f(8) = 13$ since $8 = 5 + 3$, and we can replace $3$ with $5$ to get $13$. How many integers $n$ in $S$ satisfy the property that applying $f$ repeatedly on $n$ eventually returns to $n$ after exactly 6 steps?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). If \( P(x) \) has at least one real root and the absolute value of all its coefficients is less than \( 10^{6} \), find the maximum number of distinct integer roots that \( P(x) \) can have.

Suppose we have a set of $n$ distinct positive integers. If we choose any two distinct numbers from the set, their sum is divisible by their product. What is the largest possible number of integers in the set?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 2 \) and \( P(2) = 3 \). Define the function \( Q(x) = P(P(x)) \). If \( Q(n) \) is divisible by 5 for all integers \( n \), find the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Given a set $S$ of $2023$ points in the plane, let $f(S)$ be the minimum number of triangles with vertices in $S$ such that every point in $S$ is a vertex of at least one triangle. Suppose further that no three points in $S$ are collinear. Determine the maximum value of $f(S)$ over all such sets $S$.

Alice, Bob, and Charlie are playing a game on a plane. Alice starts at point \(A\) and moves towards point \(B\), which is exactly 10 units away. Bob starts at point \(B\) and moves towards point \(C\), which is 15 units away from \(B\). Charlie starts at point \(C\) and moves directly back to point \(A\). Alice and Bob move at constant speeds such that Alice takes 3 units of time to reach \(B\) and Bob takes 5 units of time to reach \(C\). Charlie starts moving immediately after both Alice and Bob begin their journeys. If the total path length traveled by Charlie is to be exactly half the distance between points \(A\) and \(B\) plus half the distance between points \(B\) and \(C\), at what point along the path from \(C\) back to \(A\) should Charlie start to move if Alice and Bob each move directly in the direction of their respective destinations?

Let P be a regular 2023-gon with vertices labeled v_1, v_2, ..., v_{2023}. Let S be the set of all non-empty subsets of {v_1, v_2, ..., v_{2023}}. For each T in S, let w(T) be the product of the distances between every pair of distinct points in T. Define f(T) = 1/w(T) for each T in S. Determine the remainder when

\[\sum_{T \in S} f(T)\]

is divided by 1000.

Consider a sequence of integers \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots\) defined by \(a_1 = 2\), \(a_2 = 3\), and for \(n \geq 3\), \(a_n\) is the smallest positive integer greater than \(a_{n-1}\) that cannot be represented as the product of any two distinct earlier terms in the sequence. Determine \(a_{2024}\).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( n \ge 2 \), the value \( P(n) \) is divisible by a prime number \( p_n \) which is distinct from \( p_m \) for all \( m < n \). Find the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \) that satisfies these conditions.

Consider a sequence \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) where each term is a positive integer and satisfies \(a_{i+1} = a_i^2 - a_i + 1\) for \(1 \leq i < n\). Define \(S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{a_i}\). For a given integer \(k\), determine the smallest \(n\) such that \(S_n\) is an integer and \(a_1\) is a divisor of \(k\).

Let $P(x) = x^4 + ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ be a polynomial with real coefficients such that $P(1) = 2023$, $P(2) = 2024$, $P(3) = 2025$, and $P(4) = 2026$. Find the remainder when $P(5)$ is divided by 1000.

Alice and Bob play a game on a $2n \times 2n$ grid. Initially, each cell in the grid is empty. On each turn, Alice places a red token on an empty cell, and Bob places a blue token on another empty cell. The game ends when all cells have a token. At that point, Alice wins if every red token has at least one blue token on a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which Alice can guarantee a win no matter how Bob plays. If you believe the game is always a win for Bob, enter 'Bob' as the answer.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite strip of squares, numbered 0, 1, 2, and so on. Initially, each square has the number 0 written on it. Alice starts by writing a non-zero integer on any square she chooses. Bob then chooses any two different squares and switches their values. Alice then chooses any square and increases by 1 all numbers on squares whose distance from the chosen square is at most 2 (including the chosen square itself). Bob again chooses any two different squares and switches their values. Then it is again Alice's turn to increase by 1 the numbers on some squares (as described before). The game ends when all numbers on the squares are non-negative. What is the smallest possible sum of all numbers on the squares when the game ends?

A regular octagon has sides of length 2 units. If we consider all possible squares whose sides lie along these octagon's sides, let \(N\) be the maximum possible number of such squares that can be placed inside the octagon without overlapping. Calculate the remainder when \(N\) is divided by 100.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 3 \). Furthermore, suppose that for any integer \( n \), the value of \( P(n) \) is divisible by either 2 or 3. Determine all possible values of \( P(-1) \).

Consider a sequence defined recursively by \( a_0 = 2 \) and \( a_n = 2^{a_{n-1}} - 1 \) for \( n \geq 1 \). Let \( S_n \) denote the sum of the digits in the base-2 representation of \( a_n \). Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( S_n \) is divisible by 2023.
What is the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that \( \binom{n}{2} \) is divisible by 12, and the sum of all positive divisors of \( n \) is a prime number?

Let $P(x)$ be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 2023$. Furthermore, suppose that for every prime number $p$, the polynomial $P(x)$ modulo $p$ has exactly one root modulo $p$. Determine the smallest possible degree of $P(x)$.

Consider a sequence of complex numbers $\{z_n\}$ defined by $z_1 = 1 + i$ and for $n \geq 1,$
\[z_{n+1} = \frac{1 + z_n + |z_n|}{1 - z_n + |z_n|}.\]Let $P_n$ denote the product of the first $n$ terms of this sequence, i.e., $P_n = \prod_{k=1}^n z_k.$ Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that $|P_n| = 10^{2023}.$

Define a sequence $(a_n)$ by $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = \frac{1}{3}$, $a_3 = 1$, and $$a_n = \frac{2n}{3n^2 - 3n + 1} - \frac{n}{n - 1} a_{n-1} \text{ for } n > 3$$.
Find $\frac{a_1}{2} + \frac{a_2}{3} + \frac{a_3}{4} + \dotsb + \frac{a_{1000}}{1001}$.

Alice has a 10x10 grid of cells, initially all empty. She plays a game in which she can perform two types of moves: 
- **Type 1:** She can choose any row, and invert the parity of every cell in that row (i.e., if a cell was even, it becomes odd, and vice versa).
- **Type 2:** She can choose any column, and invert the parity of every cell in that column.

Alice is called **parity-proficient** if, after any series of moves, she can always set the parity of any single cell to even or odd, no matter what the current state of the grid is.

Alice is given a set of rules, each rule specifying a target parity for certain cells in the grid. She can win a prize if she can always achieve every rule's parity requirement. What is the largest number of rules such that Alice can win every rule?
Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that the product of all positive integers less than \( n \) is congruent to 2 modulo 13.

Alice has a bag of 100 marbles, each marble being either red, blue, or green. She decides to arrange them in a row following a specific pattern: a block of red marbles followed by a block of blue marbles followed by a block of green marbles, repeating this pattern exactly 10 times. If the number of red marbles is at least 30, and the number of green marbles is exactly 20, what is the smallest possible number of blue marbles she could have?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2023 \). Suppose further that for every prime number \( p \), there exists an integer \( k \) such that \( P(k) \) is divisible by \( p \) but not by \( p^2 \). Determine the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for some prime \( p \), the values \( P(k) \mod p \) for \( k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, p-1 \) are all distinct. Prove that if \( n \) is a positive integer and \( n \equiv k \pmod{p-1} \) for some \( k \) such that \( P(k) \equiv m \pmod{p} \), then \( P(n) \equiv m \pmod{p} \).

In the Cartesian plane, let $P$ be the point with coordinates $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$, and let $Q$ be the point with coordinates $(\sqrt{3}-1,\sqrt{3})$. A sequence of points $\{P_n\}$ in the plane is defined recursively by $P_0=P$, $P_{n+1}$ is the midpoint of the line segment connecting $P_n$ and $Q$, and $P_n$ is reflected over the $x$-axis before the midpoint is computed for $n \geq 1$. Find the distance between the limit point of $\{P_n\}$ and the origin.

Alice and Bob play a game on a \(10 \times 10\) grid of unit squares. They take turns placing red or blue stones on unoccupied squares, with Alice starting first. A player loses if, after placing their stone, there exist four distinct squares \(P, Q, R, S\) such that \(P, Q, R, S\) form the vertices of a rectangle with sides parallel to the grid lines, and all four of \(P, Q, R, S\) are occupied by stones of the same color. How many minimum number of moves does Alice need to make to guarantee a win, regardless of how Bob plays? (A "move" consists of placing one stone).

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 1$ and $P(2) = 2$. Suppose further that for every integer $k$, $P(k)$ divides $k^4 - k^2$. Find the number of distinct values of $P(3)$ that are possible.

Find all real numbers $x,y$ and $z$ that satisfy \begin{align*} x^2+2(x\sqrt{y}+\sqrt{y})+\frac{z^3}{3} &= 1 \\ y^2+2(y\sqrt{z}+\sqrt{z})+\frac{x^3}{3} &= 1 \\ z^2+2(z\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{x})+\frac{y^3}{3} &= 1 \end{align*}

Alice and Bob play a game with a fair coin and a sequence of integers [1, 2, ..., n] where n is an integer greater than 3. Alice chooses any two distinct positions in the sequence, and Bob tosses the coin. If it lands heads, Alice moves to the next integer following the two she selected; if tails, she moves to the previous integer. The goal is for Alice to reach either 1 or n without landing on the same integer twice. Alice cannot guarantee success in a fixed number of turns for any n. How many integer values of n less than 100 guarantee that Alice can win with her optimal strategy?

Alice and Bob play a game on an \(n \times n\) grid of squares, where \(n\) is a positive integer. Initially, the grid is entirely empty. On each turn, a player selects an empty square and places a coin on that square, marking the start of a "run". A run can be extended by placing another coin directly above, below, to the left, or to the right of the previous coin. Once a run ends (by a player deciding it's over or by reaching the grid's boundary), no more coins can be placed in that run. Each player aims to end their run with the maximum number of coins possible. The game ends when all squares are occupied by coins.

Alice and Bob take turns, starting with Alice. What is the smallest value of \(n\) such that Alice can guarantee a run with at least 2023 coins, regardless of Bob's moves?

Let \( P(x) \) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(n) \) is divisible by \( n! \) for all positive integers \( n \). Determine the smallest possible degree of \( P(x) \) and provide a polynomial of that degree satisfying these conditions.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of unit squares, where each square is colored either black or white. They start with a single black square in the center of the grid. In each turn, Alice can color any uncolored square adjacent to exactly two black squares black, and Bob can color any uncolored square adjacent to exactly three black squares black. If Alice goes first and both play optimally, for what smallest positive integer $n$ can Bob ensure that there will be at least $n$ black squares on the grid after some finite number of turns?

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2 \). Suppose further that for every integer \( n \), the value \( P(n) \) is a perfect square. Determine the minimum possible degree of such a polynomial.

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 3$. Suppose that for all positive integers $n$, there exist positive integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ such that \[P(a_1)P(a_2)\cdots P(a_n) = (P(1)P(2)\cdots P(n))^2.\] Prove that there exists a positive integer $k$ for which $P(k) = P(k-1) + 2^{k-1}$.

Alice is given a sequence of \(n\) distinct positive integers \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\). She constructs a new sequence \(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n\) where \(b_i\) is the maximum number of pairs of distinct indices \(j, k\) such that \(a_j + a_k = a_i\). Alice wants to maximize the sum of all \(b_i\). If the original sequence is chosen randomly from all permutations of \(1\) through \(n\), what is the expected value of this maximum sum?

In a given simple, connected graph with 100 vertices, where each vertex is uniquely labeled from 1 to 100 and every pair of vertices is connected by exactly one path, a "lucky vertex" is defined as a vertex whose label is a prime number and which is connected to at least one vertex with a label that is a perfect square. How many distinct simple, connected graphs can be formed under these conditions if exactly 25 of the vertices labeled from 1 to 100 are chosen to form the graph?

Alice and Bob play a game on an 8x8 chessboard. Initially, Alice places a single coin on any square. They then take turns, with Alice starting, moving the coin from its current position to a neighboring square (adjacent horizontally or vertically). The game ends when the coin reaches any square on the edge of the board. The player who moves the coin to the edge wins. If both players play optimally, determine the total number of distinct initial positions from which Alice can force a win.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of unit squares. Alice has a circular coin with a fixed radius r = 1. She places the coin such that its center is at a lattice point, and the coin completely covers a finite number of lattice points. Bob chooses an integer n ≥ 2 and adds n coins to the grid. If he can place these n coins so that every lattice point covered by the original coin is also covered by at least one of the n new coins, Bob wins. Determine the smallest n such that for any placement of Alice's coin, Bob can always win the game.

On a 2D plane, define a grid system where the origin (0,0) is not visible. An opaque rectangle with two vertices at (-10, 10) and (-12, 12), and two vertices at (10, -10) and (12, -12), is placed such that every point inside the rectangle is obscured. Now, a ray is drawn from the origin to another point \((x,y)\). If this ray cannot intersect the rectangle at any point, then \((x,y)\) is deemed "visible" from the origin. Determine the probability that a randomly chosen point \((x,y)\) from the entire infinite plane is "visible" to the origin.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(1) = 1 \) and \( P(2) = 2 \). Suppose further that for some positive integer \( k \geq 3 \), \( P(k) \) divides \( k! \). What is the largest possible value of \( k \) such that there exists a polynomial \( Q(x) \) with integer coefficients satisfying \( P(x)Q(x) = x^3 - x \)?
